accroche: Camus's most quoted sentence is the last of his book, and it does not say what you think
contenu_vulgarise:
The gods condemned Sisyphus to roll a rock to the top of a mountain, from which the stone falls back by its own weight. They had thought, Camus writes, that there is no more dreadful punishment than futile and hopeless labor.

*Le Mythe de Sisyphe* (*The Myth of Sisyphus*) appeared in 1942. It opens with an abrupt sentence, there is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide, and closes with: “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.” Between the two, a line of reasoning that is poorly summed up.

## Where the Absurd Lies

The most widespread misreading comes down to three words: “life is absurd.” Camus says something else, and he insists on it. The absurd lies neither in the world nor in man: it is born of their confrontation.

The world is not absurd; it is silent, indifferent, with no reason to give. Man is not absurd; he asks for meaning, that is his way of being. The absurd is the divorce between this demand and this silence. Remove either term and it disappears.

The nuance has consequences. If the absurd were a property of the world, there would be nothing to do with it. If it is a relation, the question becomes: how to stand within this relation without suppressing it?

## The Two Escapes He Refuses

Suppressing a term is precisely what Camus calls an escape.

Suicide suppresses the one who questions. Camus rejects it by logic, not by morality: it is to admit that life is not worth the trouble, whereas nothing establishes that.

The “leap” suppresses the silence of the world, by lending it a meaning that comes from elsewhere, religious or philosophical. Camus calls it a philosophical suicide. He does not say it is false; he says it dodges the question.

A third way remains: to hold both terms together, without consolation.

## What This Shifts

Sisyphus is therefore not happy despite his rock, and even less through the force of positive thinking. He is happy because he has ceased to hope for anything else, and because his fate, stripped of hope, belongs entirely to him.

Camus even specifies the moment that interests him: the descent, when Sisyphus goes back for his stone in full awareness. That hour of lucidity is his victory. There is no fate, he writes, that cannot be surmounted by scorn.

carte.punch: “Life is absurd” is not what Camus says.
carte.idee: The absurd lies neither in the world, which is merely silent, nor in man, who asks for meaning: it is born of their confrontation. Remove either term and it disappears. That is why Camus refuses suicide as much as consolation.

quiz.question: Where does the absurd lie, according to Camus?
choix: In the world itself, which lacks any rational order
In human nature, unable to be satisfied with its condition
In the confrontation between the demand for meaning and the silence of the world
In the certainty of death, which deprives every action of value in advance
quiz.explication: Camus insists: neither the world nor man is absurd taken separately. The absurd is the divorce between a demand for meaning and a silence, a relation, not a property. That is what makes the position tenable: one can inhabit a relation, whereas one can do nothing with a property of the world.

quiz_supplementaire.question: With which sentence does Camus open The Myth of Sisyphus?
choix: There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide
The world is absurd and so is man
There is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The book opens with an abrupt sentence, there is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide, before developing the whole line of reasoning on the absurd.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Camus reject suicide, the first of the two escapes he refuses?
choix: Out of purely personal religious conviction, which would forbid him to dispose of his own life
By logic: suicide amounts to admitting that life is not worth the trouble, whereas nothing establishes that
Out of prudence, so as not to shock his readers in 1942
Because he considers that suffering always has a hidden meaning
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Camus rejects suicide by logic and not by morality: taking one's own life amounts to admitting that it is not worth living, a conclusion that nothing allows one to establish.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which precise moment in the myth of Sisyphus does Camus single out as that of his victory?
choix: The moment when Sisyphus finally reaches the top of the mountain with his rock
The moment when the gods pronounce the sentence
The descent, when Sisyphus goes back down for his stone in full awareness
The moment when the rock falls back by its own weight
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Camus specifies that it is the descent, when Sisyphus goes back for his stone in full awareness of his fate, that constitutes his hour of lucidity and therefore his victory.
